paragraphs: The Old Clock Tower, posted by Lily. On Sunday, Mom, Tom, and I visited the old clock tower in town. The tower is more than one century old. It stands in the middle of the old town, next to the market. A woman at the desk said, "Wait a moment, and I will get your tickets." I looked at the price list on the wall.

The list said, "Normal ticket: forty baht." "Student ticket: twenty baht." "Children under six: free." "Cash only." Mom needed one normal ticket and two student tickets. "That is forty and twenty and twenty," said Tom, "so the price is eighty baht." Mom paid cash with a note of one hundred baht. She got twenty baht back. The woman gave her a small paper receipt for eighty baht.

At the desk, we could also borrow a small guidebook for the tour. It was free, but we had to return it at the end. Tom read the first page of the guidebook. "How many stairs does the tower have?" I asked. "The tower is thirty-five meters high," he read. "It has one hundred twenty stairs." "The tower has about one million small stones in its walls." "One million is a very big number," said Mom. "I do not want to count them!"

We climbed the stairs slowly. We stopped two times to rest. The stairs were small, but the walls were cool. At the top, we saw the big clock from inside. The clock face is three meters wide. Each number on the clock is as tall as my arm, and it is painted black. Tom stood next to the number five, and I stood next to the number six. The clock has a big bell. It rings every hour.

At twelve o'clock, the bell rang twelve times. We stood on the top floor and listened to the loud sound. The normal opening hours of the tower are from nine o'clock to five o'clock. "I like the view, because I can see our school," said Tom. "I can see the park, too," I said. We took photos of the town for Explorers' Blog. Then we walked down the stairs and returned the guidebook at the desk. Mom kept the receipt in her bag. She smiled at us.
